title: WHY DOES LUST FEEL SO POWERFUL? THE SECRET BATTLE THAT CAN DESTROY YOU EVEN WHILE YOU STILL LOVE JESUS
paragraphs: WHY DOES LUST FEEL SO POWERFUL? THE SECRET BATTLE THAT CAN DESTROY YOU EVEN WHILE YOU STILL LOVE JESUS

You can love God, know the Scriptures, worship with tears in your eyes, and still find yourself fighting desires you are ashamed to confess. But what if the deepest danger isn't simply what lust makes you want—it's what lust makes you believe you cannot live without?
There is a moment in the life of almost every struggling believer that nobody sees.
The room is quiet.
The phone is within reach.
The world has gone to sleep.
And something inside you begins negotiating with everything you promised God you would never do again.
You remember the last time.
The guilt afterward. The heaviness in your chest. The prayer you whispered with tears in your eyes.
“Lord, please. I don't want to keep living like this.”
You meant it.
You genuinely meant it.
But now the temptation has returned, and somehow the promises you made in yesterday's tears seem weaker than the desires confronting you tonight.
You know what Scripture says.
You know where this road leads.
You know that temporary pleasure has repeatedly left you feeling spiritually empty.
And yet something keeps pulling.
Something keeps whispering.
Just one more time.
You've already failed so many times. What difference will one more failure make?
Nobody will know.
And perhaps the most frightening thought of all:
What if I never change?
If you recognize this battle, stay with me.
Because we need to talk about something deeper than pornography, sexual fantasies, inappropriate relationships, secret messages, or the images people hide behind locked screens.
We need to talk about why lust can feel so powerful that even people who sincerely love Jesus sometimes find themselves surrendering to it.
And we need to confront a truth that may disturb you before it sets you free.
Lust does not become powerful merely because you desire something. It becomes dangerous when desire begins demanding the obedience that belongs to God.
But there is another truth.
One that shame desperately wants you to forget.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross because humanity was already clean.
He went because sinners needed a Savior.
And that includes people fighting battles they are terrified to admit.
The Bible never pretends that sexual temptation is a small matter.
Jesus spoke about it with breathtaking seriousness.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He said:
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart.” (WEB)
The original Greek expression is particularly revealing.
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
pros to epithymēsai autēn
In this context, the phrase refers to looking at someone with lustful desire.

The verb epithymeō means to desire or long for something. The word itself does not always describe sinful desire. In Luke 22:15, Jesus uses the same Greek verb when expressing His earnest desire to eat the Passover with His disciples.
That distinction matters.
Because not every desire is sin.
Not every experience of attraction is rebellion.
Not every unwanted sexual thought means you have deliberately committed adultery in your heart.
Jesus is confronting the deliberate cultivation of lustful desire—the inward choice to turn another person into an object of sexual gratification outside God's righteous purposes.
He is exposing the heart behind the outward action.
And suddenly, the question becomes painfully personal.
What do you do with the second look?
What happens when you choose to entertain the fantasy?
What happens when your imagination begins rehearsing what your conscience knows you should refuse?
What happens when another human being, made in God's image, becomes something you mentally consume rather than someone you recognize as worthy of dignity?
This is where lust begins revealing its spiritual danger.
It promises intimacy without covenant.
Pleasure without responsibility.
Possession without love.
Satisfaction without surrender.
And for a brief moment, it can feel convincing.
But lust is a terrible substitute for love.
Love recognizes the dignity of another person.
Lust, when cultivated sinfully, reduces that person to the satisfaction of an appetite.
Love is willing to sacrifice.
Lust demands to be satisfied.
Love can wait.
Lust insists that waiting is unbearable.
And when lust becomes habitual, it can begin shaping the way a person thinks, responds, remembers, and seeks comfort.
That is one reason the battle can feel so overwhelming.

Our brains are designed to respond to rewarding experiences. Sexual stimulation can activate neural systems involved in motivation, anticipation, and reward. Repeated behaviors can also become associated with familiar cues—stress, loneliness, boredom, particular images, certain times of day, or simply being alone with a phone.
This does not mean every person experiencing sexual desire has an addiction.
It does not mean the brain has been permanently damaged.
And it certainly does not mean transformation is impossible.
It means human behavior involves the body, mind, habits, relationships, and choices.
Sometimes a person reaches for sexual stimulation because they are seeking pleasure.
Sometimes because they are escaping discomfort.
Sometimes because loneliness has become unbearable.
Sometimes because anxiety feels louder than their ability to cope.
And sometimes because a familiar behavior has become an automatic response to a familiar situation.
Not every struggle has the same cause.
But every believer needs to understand this:
A desire can feel urgent without being a command you must obey.
The apostle James explains something profoundly important.
In James 1:14–15, he writes:
The Greek word translated here as “lust” is:
ἐπιθυμία — epithymia
It means desire or longing. Depending on context, it may refer to good desires or sinful cravings.
In James's warning, the desire has become disordered. It entices a person toward sin.
Notice the progression.
Temptation.
Enticement.
Sin.
Death.
James does not say that merely experiencing temptation is the same as surrendering to it.
That distinction is essential.
Hebrews 4:15 teaches that Jesus was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
Temptation itself is not proof that God has abandoned you.
The presence of a battle does not automatically mean you have lost it.
But James warns that when sinful desire is welcomed, nourished, and obeyed, it can grow into destructive behavior.
And that is precisely why the seemingly harmless private compromises matter.
The image you return to.
The conversation you know is becoming inappropriate.
The fantasy you deliberately keep alive.
The account you refuse to unfollow.
The secrecy you defend because exposing it would require change.
Sin rarely announces its final destination when it first knocks on the door.
It asks for something small.
A moment.
A glance.
A little secrecy.
A harmless exception.
And gradually, what once troubled your conscience can begin to feel normal.
This is not because God has stopped speaking.
Sometimes it is because you have practiced ignoring what you already know.
And that should concern us.
Not because grace has run out.
But because sin is never as harmless as it wants to appear.
Consider King David.
A man after God's own heart.
A worshiper.
A warrior.
A king who knew what it meant to depend upon the Lord.
And yet in 2 Samuel 11, David saw Bathsheba bathing.
The tragedy was not simply that David noticed her beauty.
David inquired about her.
He learned she was married.
He sent for her anyway.
He abused his royal power, committed adultery, and later arranged the circumstances that led to her husband Uriah's death.
We must not romanticize this story as an ordinary love affair. The account exposes David's grave abuse of authority and the devastating harm caused by his choices.
The man who had defeated Goliath could not excuse his sin by pointing to his earlier victories.
His spiritual history did not make him immune to moral failure.
His position did not make his actions righteous.
And his private desires did not entitle him to another person's body.
Think about that.
You can defeat enormous battles in public and still be dangerously careless in private.
You can know how to worship and still need to repent.
You can have a history of spiritual victories and still face a temptation that demands vigilance today.
But David's story does not end with his sin being concealed.
God sent the prophet Nathan to confront him.
And David was brought face-to-face with the truth.
In Psalm 51:10, traditionally associated with David's repentance, we find this prayer:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (WEB)
In Hebrew:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
The Hebrew verb בָּרָא — bara means “to create.”
David is not merely asking for a better reputation.
He is asking God for inward renewal.
He is not asking for a way to make the consequences disappear.
He is asking for a clean heart.
And perhaps that is the prayer some of us have been avoiding.
Because we have been asking God to remove the consequences of our sin while resisting the surrender that genuine repentance requires.
We want the guilt to stop.
But do we want the behavior to stop?
We want peace.
But are we willing to bring the hidden things into the light?
We want freedom.
But do we keep protecting the very patterns that are enslaving us?
Those questions are uncomfortable.
They are supposed to be.
Conviction is not meant to entertain us.
It is meant to turn us toward the truth.
Yet conviction and condemnation are not the same thing.
Conviction exposes sin and calls us toward repentance.
Condemnation tells us that we are beyond the reach of mercy.
And Scripture does not permit us to confuse those two voices.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.” (WEB)
Read that again.
No condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because holiness is optional.
But because Christ has done what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He bore sin.
He died.
He rose again.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered by grace.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than religious information.
It becomes the difference between despair and hope.
Because perhaps your deepest struggle is no longer merely the temptation itself.
Perhaps it is the identity you have built around your failures.
You have begun calling yourself filthy.
Disgusting.
Hopeless.
A hypocrite.
Someone God must be tired of hearing from.
You have mistaken the repetition of your sin for proof that your entire life is beyond redemption.
But listen carefully.
Your sin must be confronted.
Your excuses must be abandoned.
Your actions may require confession, accountability, restitution, and serious change.
But your failures do not possess greater saving power than the finished work of Jesus Christ.
The cross is not permission to continue in sin.
It is the place where the sinner discovers both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing mercy of God.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
Paul's answer is emphatic:
“May it never be!”
Grace is not a spiritual loophole.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings us into a new relationship with Him and teaches us to reject ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 makes that connection clear.
God's grace does not merely forgive.
It also trains.
It transforms.
It calls us into a different way of living.
And this is where the battle against lust begins to change.
Not when you convince yourself that you are strong enough to resist every temptation alone.
But when you stop pretending that secret compromise can coexist peacefully with wholehearted surrender.
You begin taking Jesus seriously.
You begin taking your choices seriously.
You begin treating the people you encounter as image-bearers rather than instruments of gratification.
You begin recognizing that holiness is not hatred of the body.
It is learning to honor God with the body.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 that believers' bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit and that they are to glorify God in their bodies.
The human body is not inherently dirty.
Sexuality is not inherently evil.
God created human beings as embodied persons, and Scripture honors sexual union within marriage.
The problem is not that God created desire.
The problem arises when desire is directed toward what God forbids or elevated above obedience to Him.
This is why biblical purity cannot be reduced to fear of sexuality.
It is about rightly ordered love.
It is about faithfulness.
It is about honoring people rather than exploiting them.
It is about learning to say no to what promises immediate pleasure at the cost of obedience, integrity, and love.
And sometimes, that obedience becomes painfully practical.
It means deleting what keeps drawing you back.
Ending the private conversation that has crossed appropriate boundaries.
Choosing not to browse aimlessly when you know you are vulnerable.
Putting your phone away when exhaustion has weakened your judgment.
Speaking honestly with a mature, trustworthy Christian who can offer prayer and accountability without humiliation.

And when the behavior has become persistent, compulsive, or deeply distressing, it may mean seeking help from a qualified mental health professional who can address the underlying patterns without dismissing your faith.
None of these actions purchases salvation.
None of them replaces dependence upon Christ.
They are practical ways of refusing to make provision for sin.
Romans 13:14 says:
“But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts.” (WEB)
The original Greek includes:
μὴ πρόνοιαν ποιεῖσθε
mē pronoian poieisthe
“Do not make provision.”
In context, Paul is warning believers not to plan ahead for the gratification of sinful desires.
That is a sobering thought.
Sometimes we pray to overcome temptation while quietly arranging the conditions that make surrender more likely.
We ask God for strength while keeping the door open.
We ask for deliverance while protecting the pathway back.
But genuine repentance begins changing the direction of our decisions.
Not perfectly.
Not always instantly.
But sincerely.
And the beautiful thing about Christian growth is that the Holy Spirit does not merely command believers to become different.
He works within them.
Galatians 5:16 calls Christians to walk by the Spirit rather than fulfill the lust of the flesh.
The word “walk” communicates an ongoing manner of life.
Not one emotional moment.
Not one dramatic prayer.
Not one night of tears.
A continuing life of dependence, obedience, repentance, and faith.
There may be days when the temptation feels loud.
There may be moments when old memories return.
There may be situations when you need to leave the room, call someone, close the application, or redirect your attention before a passing thought becomes a deliberate choice.
And there may be failures that require you to confess honestly, seek forgiveness, and make changes rather than collapse into despair.
Christian maturity is not pretending that temptation has disappeared.
It is learning to respond to temptation with truth, wisdom, self-control, and dependence upon God.
And there is something else we must say.
You are not required to hate yourself in order to hate your sin.
Some believers have spent years confusing shame with holiness.
They believe that if they punish themselves emotionally enough, perhaps God will finally consider their repentance sincere.
But self-hatred is not the price of forgiveness.
Jesus already paid the price of redemption through His death.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (WEB)
Notice whose faithfulness the promise emphasizes.
His.
God's faithfulness.
God's righteousness.
God's willingness to forgive those who confess their sins.
That promise is not an invitation to perform the same sin without repentance.
It is an invitation to stop hiding.
To come into the light.
To tell the truth.
To abandon the lie that secrecy will protect you.
And perhaps the hardest part of coming into the light is realizing that you cannot build a transformed life while continually defending an unchanged heart.
You may need to admit that what you have been calling “just stress relief” has become a destructive pattern.
You may need to acknowledge that the relationship you have been justifying is violating your commitments.
You may need to stop blaming the internet, your loneliness, your spouse, your past, or other people's appearances for choices that belong to you.
Your circumstances may help explain why the temptation feels powerful.
They do not automatically excuse your response.
And yet, even here, Christ calls you toward something greater than endless self-accusation.
He calls you to Himself.
Remember the woman brought before Jesus in John 8?
Her accusers wanted to use her situation as a trap.
Jesus exposed their hypocrisy.
And when the accusers departed, He did not tell the woman that sin no longer mattered.
He told her:
“Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” (John 8:11, WEB)
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin behind.
Compassion.
And a summons to change.
That is the beauty of Christ.
He does not need to minimize sin in order to show mercy.
He does not need to abandon righteousness in order to welcome the repentant.
And He does not need to destroy a wounded person in order to confront what is destroying them.
There is a tenderness in the Savior that many ashamed believers have forgotten.
He knows the truth about humanity.
He knows the secrets people conceal.
He knows the sins that have left families broken, relationships wounded, and consciences burdened.
And still, the Gospel announces that sinners can be reconciled to God through Him.
Not through their moral résumé.
Not through religious performance.
Not through a streak of perfect behavior.
Through Jesus Christ.
But that reconciliation is not merely a change in how we are regarded.
It brings us into a new life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (WEB)
This does not mean every habit disappears overnight.
It does not mean every consequence vanishes.
It does not mean believers become incapable of temptation.
It means that union with Christ brings a fundamentally new identity and direction.
You no longer have to define yourself by the worst thing you have done.
You are called to live in the light of the One who died and rose again.
And perhaps that is what lust has been stealing from you.
Not merely your time.
Not merely your concentration.
Not merely the peace you feel after prayer.
Perhaps it has been persuading you to live as though your appetites are your master and your past is your future.
But the Gospel tells another story.
Sin is a terrible master.
Christ is a sufficient Savior.
And the person who turns to Him in repentance and faith is not condemned to remain under the dominion of sin.
So tonight, if temptation returns, remember this.
You do not have to negotiate with every thought.
You do not have to entertain every image.
You do not have to obey every urge.
You do not have to prove your strength by remaining close to what repeatedly draws you into sin.
You can flee.
You can pray.
You can seek help.
You can choose what is right even when your emotions have not caught up with your convictions.
First Corinthians 10:13 teaches that God is faithful and will not allow believers to be tempted beyond what they can bear, but will provide a way to endure temptation.
That promise is not a guarantee that temptation will feel easy.
It is a reminder that temptation does not possess unlimited authority over the believer.
And sometimes the way of escape looks very ordinary.
Turning off the screen.
Leaving the conversation.
Getting out of bed.
Calling a trusted friend.
Remembering the Scriptures.
Choosing to sleep instead of feeding a destructive cycle.
Ordinary acts of obedience can become meaningful moments of spiritual resistance.
Do not despise them because they are not dramatic.
A changed life is often built through repeated acts of faithfulness that nobody applauds.
And if you have already fallen?
Do not turn one failure into permission for another.
Do not use grace as an excuse.
But do not treat despair as repentance either.
Confess.
Turn back.
Make the necessary changes.
Receive the forgiveness Christ offers.
And continue walking with Him.
Because the goal is not simply to become a person who never looks at something inappropriate.
The goal is to become a person whose heart increasingly loves what God loves.
A person who can recognize beauty without demanding possession.
A person who can experience loneliness without using another human being as an escape.
A person who can face discomfort without automatically reaching for secret gratification.
A person who values faithfulness more than fleeting pleasure.
A person who sees holiness not as a prison but as the freedom to belong wholeheartedly to Jesus Christ.
And perhaps, as you read this, you are realizing something you have never admitted aloud.
You are exhausted.
Not merely from temptation.
From hiding.
From making promises and breaking them.
From smiling at church while carrying private guilt.
From wondering whether the people who admire your faith would still respect you if they knew your struggle.
From fearing that God must be disappointed every time you come back to Him.
If that is you, please hear this.
You do not need another performance.
You need truth.
You need repentance.
You need the grace of Jesus Christ.
You need a life where your private choices increasingly agree with the faith you publicly confess.
And you may need other trustworthy believers to walk beside you while that change takes shape.
There is no spiritual award for struggling alone.
James 5:16 encourages believers to confess their sins to one another and pray for one another.
That does not mean broadcasting intimate details to strangers.
It means rejecting the isolation that allows sin to flourish unchecked.
Find someone mature, discreet, compassionate, and grounded in Scripture.
Someone who will neither excuse your behavior nor reduce your identity to it.
Someone who will remind you of Christ when shame tries to erase hope.
Someone who will ask difficult questions because your spiritual well-being matters.
And remember that real repentance includes how we treat others.
If your actions have harmed someone, repentance may require acknowledging that harm, respecting their boundaries, and accepting appropriate consequences.
Forgiveness from God does not entitle anyone to immediate restoration of another person's trust.
Grace teaches responsibility.
Love refuses exploitation.
Holiness protects the dignity of others.
That is part of what it means to follow Jesus.
Now I want to ask you something.
Not as someone standing above your struggle.
But as someone inviting you to stand honestly before the Lord.
What would change if you stopped asking only, “How do I make this temptation disappear?” and started asking, “Jesus, what are You teaching me to love more than this?”
What if your next prayer was not simply about escaping consequences?
What if it was about surrendering the hidden parts of your life?
What if the place where you have experienced your deepest shame became the place where you began learning the depth of God's grace?
Not because the sin was good.
But because Christ is merciful.
Because He restores repentant sinners.
Because He makes new what sin has damaged.
Because the Gospel does not end with humanity's rebellion.
It announces the death and resurrection of the Redeemer.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not that scandal is harmless.
It is that scandal does not have to be the final word over a repentant life.
From Scandal to Grace is not a promise that your past never happened. It is the testimony that Jesus Christ can redeem a life that sin could never repair.
And this is why we continue writing, teaching, sharing Scripture, and creating resources that call people beyond temporary inspiration into genuine discipleship.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is staring at a screen and wondering whether they are too far gone.
Someone is fighting the same temptation for the hundredth time.
Someone is carrying a secret that has become heavier than they can bear.
Someone has mistaken their repeated failure for proof that Jesus has stopped calling them.
And someone desperately needs to hear that repentance is still possible, grace is still real, and Christ is still worthy of their surrender.
Maybe that person is you.
Or maybe that person is someone on your Facebook friends list.
Not because public engagement earns God's favor.
But because biblical truth can reach people who would never admit they were searching for it.
One thoughtful share may place this message before someone who has been suffering in silence.
One personal tag may remind a struggling friend that they are not forgotten.
One honest conversation may help someone find the courage to seek accountability and healing.

If someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sending this privately with compassion, or tagging them if you know they would welcome it. Never use another person's struggle as a public spectacle.
And if this article exposed something in your own heart, I want to invite you to respond.
You do not need to reveal intimate details.
You do not need to confess private sins to the internet.
But you can make a simple declaration of faith.
Let the comment section become a place of compassion, Scripture, encouragement, and prayer rather than judgment or humiliation.
And if God has been teaching you what genuine repentance looks like, your testimony may help someone who has forgotten that change is possible.
Not as a religious trophy.
Return to the Scriptures.
Read them in context.
Pray through them.
Allow God's Word to challenge your excuses and strengthen your hope.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, people who have drifted from church, and those still seeking to understand Jesus to follow as well.
The Gospel is too important to keep hidden behind religious appearances.
And if this ministry has genuinely helped you grow in Christ, I also want to invite you to consider something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is working to continue and expand its ministry of Scripture-centered writing, discipleship, encouragement, and Christian resources.
These resources are intended to encourage serious study, spiritual maturity, and faithful Christian living.

It can support the continued creation of biblical articles, the development of discipleship materials, the expansion of the resource library, and efforts to reach more people with the message of Christ.
But let us keep this biblically clear.

Scripture teaches believers to give willingly and cheerfully, not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). Christian giving should also reflect wise stewardship and the responsibilities God has already entrusted to us.
You do not need to pay Gospel Warrior to glorify God.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, and a life increasingly surrendered to Him.
But if you believe this ministry is faithfully serving that purpose, your voluntary support can become one practical way of participating in its mission.
And that participation matters.
Because while one person writes, another shares.
While one person gives, another prays.
While one person teaches, another quietly receives the encouragement they desperately needed.
We do not all serve in the same way.
But we can each consider how to use what God has entrusted to us for His glory.
These products are not the reason to follow Jesus.
They are simply an additional way for the ministry to thank those who voluntarily support its work.
The Gospel is not for sale.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
The blood of Jesus is not a membership benefit.
Salvation is the gift of God through faith in Jesus Christ, not the reward for financial support (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Your prayer matters.
Your faithful sharing matters.
Your encouragement of another believer matters.
Your willingness to live out the truth matters.
It is surrendering your life to Jesus Christ.
Because after the last comment has been written, the last share has been made, and the last notification has disappeared, one question will remain.
Who rules your heart?
The desire that promises everything and cannot save you?
Or the Savior who gave Himself for sinners and rose again so that those who belong to Him might walk in newness of life?
Perhaps tonight you will still feel the pull of temptation.
Perhaps tomorrow will require another difficult decision.
Perhaps the road toward lasting change will involve tears, accountability, setbacks, repentance, and the patient rebuilding of habits that have shaped your life for years.
But do not confuse a difficult road with an absent Savior.
Keep your eyes on Jesus.
Keep returning to His Word.
Keep walking in the light.
And when shame tells you that your story has already been written, remember that the risen Christ is greater than the sins you bring to Him in repentance.
He does not promise that following Him will be effortless.
He promises something infinitely better.
Himself.
So bring Him the truth.
Not the edited version.
Not the polished testimony.
Not the carefully managed image.
Bring Him the heart that needs cleansing.
Bring Him the habits that need confronting.
Bring Him the desires that need reordering.
Bring Him the failures you can no longer justify.
And ask Him to make you holy.
Not merely respectable.
Not merely religious.
Holy.
Because the greatest victory over lust is not simply reaching a day when you no longer feel temptation.
It is learning, by the grace of God, that your desires do not have to be your master.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And the life surrendered to Him can become a testimony of repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and genuine transformation.
If you can only pray one sentence tonight, let it be this:
“Lord Jesus, I am tired of hiding. Forgive me, cleanse my heart, teach me to walk in Your truth, and help me love You more than the sin that keeps calling my name. Amen.”
And when you finish that prayer, do not merely close your eyes and hope everything changes.
Open them.
Take the next faithful step.
Because grace does not call you to remain where sin left you.
It calls you to follow the Savior who came to bring you home.
The darkest chapter of your life does not have to become the final sentence of your story—because the hands that were pierced for your sins are still the hands of your Redeemer.
